Vemuram browse by type distortion/fuzz/overdrive fuzz browse by enclosure pedal Vemuram Myriad Fuzz Published on January 3, 2019 Vemuram fuzz pedal Information Vemuram Pedals Vemuram Myriad Fuzz Pedal The Vemuram  Myriad Fuzz pedal was designed in collaboration with Josh Smith. It's a hybrid-transistor design, with both a Silicon transistor and a vintage Germanium transistor, delivering a vast range of tone. It has enough headroom to take your tone from splatty fuzz, all the way to a smooth overdrive. It features a trimmer that allows you to control the Germanium Bias with the Feel knob. sources.excerpt: Vemuram Myriad Fuzz: Josh Smith's Hybrid Fuzz Beast Skip to content Dirty Guitar Facts. Loud Legends. R ock G uitars S tories P eople F orever Search GuitarGangsters ⌕ Menu Home Guitar Legends Gear & Rigs Guitars Amps Pedals & FX Pickups Accessories DIY Builds Custom Builds Electronics & Wiring Finishing & Relics Mods & Upgrades Rock History 70’s Rock 80’s Metal 90’s Grunge & Alternative 2000’s Revival News & Culture Videos About Contact In this guide The short version Who Josh Smith is, and why the pedal exists Where the Myriad Fuzz came from Specifications What every control does What it actually sounds like Famous players: what actually holds up Six settings that work How it compares Buying guide Living with one FAQ In this guide The short version Who Josh Smith is, and why the pedal exists Where the Myriad Fuzz came from Specifications What every control does What it actually sounds like Famous players: what actually holds up Six settings that work How it compares Buying guide Living with one FAQ Share this article Home › Gear & Rigs › Vemuram Myriad Fuzz: The Brass Box That Started Life As Half Of Something Bigger Gear & Rigs Vemuram Myriad Fuzz: The Brass Box That Started Life As Half Of Something Bigger Vemuram Myriad Fuzz guide: the germanium-silicon hybrid explained, the bias trimmer decoded, verified players, tone settings and 2026 buying advice. admin 22 September 2026 22 min read GG-ARTICLE-TOP Almost every fuzz pedal ever built is an argument about one transistor family. Germanium is warm, woolly, temperature-flaky and cleans up like a dream. Silicon is loud, spitty, aggressive and reliable. You pick a side, you buy the pedal, and you spend the next decade quietly wishing it did the other thing on Tuesdays. GG-ARTICLE-AFTER-INTRO The Vemuram Myriad Fuzz refuses to pick. It puts a silicon transistor and a vintage germanium transistor in the same signal path, gives you a knob called Feel to move between their characters, and hides a trimmer inside the enclosure that biases the germanium side to taste. It is hand-built in Tokyo, wrapped in solid brass, and it costs more than most people’s first amplifier. It is also, unusually for a signature pedal, the leftover half of a much stranger machine — and the guitarist whose name is on it has been photographed using it on his own board for years, which is more than can be said for a lot of endorsements. This is the full story: where the circuit came from, what every control actually does, who genuinely plays one, how to dial it in, and whether the brass justifies the invoice. How to Get the Tone ↓ The short version The Myriad Fuzz is a hybrid germanium/silicon fuzz, hand-built by Vemuram in Tokyo in a solid brass enclosure, developed with American blues guitarist and producer Josh Smith. It has four external knobs — Level, Fuzz, Feel and Tone — plus an internal Germanium Bias trimmer. It runs on a 9-volt battery or a standard centre-negative 9 V supply, is true bypass, and draws a startlingly small amount of current. Its selling point is range. At low Fuzz settings with the Feel knob backed off it behaves like a thick, saturated overdrive with enormous output on tap. Wound up, it goes into Big Muff territory without the mid-scoop, and it retains a low end that vintage Fuzz Face circuits simply do not have. It cleans up off the guitar volume knob the way good germanium fuzzes do, but it does it without the volume drop and tonal collapse that usually comes with that trick. As of September 2026 it is a $435-and-up pedal in the United States, with Equipboard tracking an average across merchants of $462 and a spread up to roughly $558. It sits in the top price tier of the fuzz category, and it knows it. Who Josh Smith is, and why the pedal exists The résumé Josh Smith was born in Middletown, Connecticut on 7 October 1979 and raised in Fort Lauderdale, Florida.
